procedural_history.impugned_order: Order framing charges against the appellants and dismissing their application for seeking discharge.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The appellants were unable to appeal to the High Court to quash the chargesheet or interfere with the order on charge due to the nature of the investigation or trial in a matter relating to coal.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellants approached the Supreme Court directly by invoking Article 136 of the Constitution of India and filing a petition for special leave to challenge the impugned orders passed by the Special Judge, CBI. A similar petition for special leave to appeal filed by accused No. 1 to 5 (functionaries of KPCL) was dismissed as withdrawn on 09th February, 2024.

directions: The order on charge dated 24th December, 2021 and the order framing charges dated 3rd March, 2022 passed by the learned Special Judge, CBI qua the appellants before this Court are unsustainable and accordingly quashed and set aside.

issue.issue_text: Whether the order framing charges against the appellants was sustainable in law.

facts: The appellants were charged by a Special Judge, CBI, under various sections of the IPC and the Prevention of Corruption Act.
This order was passed after the appellants' application for discharge under Section 227 of the Criminal Procedure Code was dismissed.
The CBI's case was primarily based on an Audit Report from the Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG).
The appellants challenged the order framing charges before the Supreme Court.
law: Under Section 227 of the Criminal Procedure Code, a judge, when considering framing charges, has the power to sift and weigh the evidence for the limited purpose of determining if a prima facie case exists against the accused.

The Supreme Court has extraordinary powers under Article 136 of the Constitution to interfere in a case, even after charges have been framed, if there are glaring infirmities in the lower court's orders.
application: The Court found that the CBI had engaged in a "roving and fishing inquiry" based on the CAG's Audit Report, which had not even attained finality.
It concluded that the CBI worked "backwards to sniff out criminal intent" in what was essentially a civil dispute arising from a contract between the parties.
The Court held that the CBI had unjustifiably "painted with the brush of criminality" a civil matter, whose breach would at most lead to the termination of the contract, not criminal proceedings.
The CBI achieved this by misinterpreting the clauses of the agreements and relying heavily on the inconclusive audit report.
The Court determined that the lower court's orders framing the charges showed a lack of proper consideration and had "glaring infirmities."
Due to these infirmities, the Court decided it was necessary to exercise its extraordinary powers under Article 136 to intervene.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the order framing charges against the appellants was unsustainable in law. It held that the CBI had wrongly converted a civil, contractual dispute into a criminal case based on a non-final audit report. Therefore, the Court quashed and set aside the order on charge and the order framing charges.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The Supreme Court found the order framing charges to be unsustainable because the prosecution was based on a CAG report. The Court had already held in a previous, related proceeding involving the same parties that this specific CAG report could not form the basis for launching proceedings against the appellants.
legal_tests_applied: A report of the Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG) cannot be the sole basis for launching a prosecution, particularly when the report has not been scrutinized by the Public Accounts Committee or Joint Parliamentary Committee and tabled before the legislature.

The inherent power of a High Court under Section 482 Cr.P.C. can be exercised to quash a proceeding if allowing it to continue would be an abuse of the process of the Court or if the ends of justice require it.
why_respondent_won: The prosecution was based on a CAG Report, but the Supreme Court had previously held in a related matter that this specific report could not form the basis for launching proceedings against the appellants.

The CAG report, which formed the basis of the prosecution, had not been accepted by the Public Accounts Committee, the Committee of Public Undertakings, or the Joint Parliamentary Committee, nor had it been tabled before Parliament, which is a necessary procedural step before it can form the basis for initiating action.
policy_considerations: The saving of the High Court’s inherent powers is designed to achieve a salutary public purpose, which is that a court proceeding ought not to be permitted to degenerate into a weapon of harassment or persecution.
Quashing a criminal proceeding where it is clear that it would not conclude in a conviction saves precious court time and does justice to the accused.
